source: Aamodt & Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches (AI Communications)
finding: Defines the 4R cycle and RETAIN as its fourth step. Retain means choosing what to keep from a solved episode, in what form, how to index it, and how to integrate it. The case base is updated no matter how the problem was solved. Failures may also be kept, as separate failure cases or inside whole cases.
numbers: Retain has four sub-tasks: extract, index, integrate, test. Candidates to extract: problem descriptors, solution, and a justification of why it is a solution. Index strengths are raised when a feature led to a successful retrieval and lowered when it led to a failed one. CASEY keeps its causal explanation inside each case.
quote: Failures, i.e. information from the Revise task, may also be extracted and retained, either as separate failure cases or within total-problem cases.
limits: A 1994 framework paper, no experiments. It lists what to store but gives no rule for which new cases to skip. The later deletion and addition policies fill that gap.
agent_relevance: This is the textbook definition of our S9 step. A case record should hold the problem, the solution, a reason why it worked, and index keys. The paper also supports storing failures with a link to the failing situation.

source: Smyth & Keane (1995) Remembering to Forget: a competence-preserving case deletion policy for CBR systems (IJCAI-95)
finding: Names the swamping problem: a growing case base slows retrieval, so cases must be dropped. Shows that the standard utility-based deletion policy (Minton) and random deletion both lose competence, meaning the share of target problems the system can still solve. Proposes the competence footprint: delete auxiliary cases first, then support, spanning, and pivotal cases last.
numbers: Setup: residential property valuation CBR, nearest-neighbour retrieval, initial case base of 50 cases, 160 target problems, benchmark competence 100%, swamping limit 75 cases (experiment 1). Case categories in that base: 20 pivotal, 5 auxiliary, 25 support (in 7 support groups), 0 spanning. Minimum competence-preserving base: 27 cases (20 pivotal + 7 support groups).
limits: One small domain. Coverage and reachability sets are computed on the same case base; assumes target problems resemble the stored cases.
agent_relevance: The key idea for S9 is that a case's value is its unique coverage, not how often it was used. A case that no other stored case could solve is pivotal and must be kept.

source: Smyth & Keane (1995) Remembering to Forget: a competence-preserving case deletion policy for CBR systems (IJCAI-95)
finding: Experiment 1: competence depletion over time once the size limit is hit. Footprint deletion (FD) and footprint-utility deletion (FUD) held competence at 100%. Utility-based deletion fell to 80% of its former level and random deletion fell to 86%. The drop began almost at once after the limit was reached, after 25 trials.
numbers: Utility deletion final competence 80%; random deletion 86%; FD and FUD 100%. Limit 75 cases, 160 target problems. Single run per policy as reported.
quote: competence had fallen to 80% and 86% of its former level for the utility and random deletion policies
limits: No error bars or repeated seeds reported. Random deletion beating utility deletion suggests utility actively removes rare but needed cases.
agent_relevance: A usage-count or recency rule can quietly delete the one example that covers a rare problem type. Check uniqueness of coverage before dropping anything.

source: Smyth & Keane (1995) Remembering to Forget: a competence-preserving case deletion policy for CBR systems (IJCAI-95)
finding: Experiment 2: vary the swamping limit from 5 to 95 cases and record final competence. The footprint policies reach about 90% of benchmark competence at a limit just over 25 cases. Random and utility deletion reach only about 60% at the same limit. The footprint policies seek out the cases with the largest competence contributions.
numbers: At limit about 25 cases: FD and FUD about 90%, random and utility about 60%. Range tested 5 to 95 cases.
limits: Values read from the text, not a table. Same single domain as experiment 1.
agent_relevance: At a tight memory budget, the choice of what to keep matters most. A small case base chosen by coverage beats a bigger one chosen by use.

source: Minton (1990) Quantitative results concerning the utility of explanation-based learning (Artificial Intelligence 42), as described in Smyth & Keane 1995
finding: The utility problem: learned knowledge can cost more to search than it saves. Utility = (application frequency x average savings) minus match cost. Items with negative utility are deleted. Smyth and Keane adopt this as the baseline utility deletion policy and show it harms competence.
numbers: Formula: Utility = (ApplicationFreq * AverageSavings) - MatchCost. No new numbers.
limits: Known only through the Smyth and Keane description; Minton's original paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: A speed-oriented rule. Our agent's concern is accuracy, so use utility only to break ties among cases that cover the same ground, as the FUD hybrid does.

source: Smyth & Keane (1995) Remembering to Forget: a competence-preserving case deletion policy for CBR systems (IJCAI-95)
finding: Formal competence model. Coverage of a case is the set of target problems it can solve. Reachability of a target is the set of cases that can solve it. Cases fall in four classes: pivotal (only they cover some problem), auxiliary (fully subsumed by another case), spanning (link otherwise separate regions), support (groups of cases with overlapping coverage). A heuristic update rule keeps these classes current as cases are learned.
numbers: Algorithm 1 (LearningUpdate) updates classes at learning time. Algorithms 2 and 3 give the footprint deletion order: auxiliary, support, spanning, pivotal. FUD uses utility inside each class to choose which to drop.
limits: The class labels are approximations: the heuristics assume the target problems are well represented by the case base, which the authors note.
agent_relevance: For LLM cases, covers can be tested by checking whether a new case's problem is already solved when its nearest stored neighbour is used. If yes, the new case is auxiliary and need not be stored.

source: Yang & Zhu (2001) A case-addition policy for case-base maintenance, Computational Intelligence 17(2)
finding: Reverses the problem from deleting to adding. A greedy case-addition algorithm picks the case with the largest additional coverage (benefit), then repeats. It is proven to return a case base whose coverage is within a fixed lower bound of the optimum, and it is more efficient than deletion. Key quantity: how fast the benefit of each added case shrinks.
numbers: The proof ends in a bound of the form Coverage >= R(2 - R) for optimal coverage R (as extracted from the PDF text; check the original for the exact constant). Under linear benefit decline, about 15% of cases give about 50% coverage and 50% of cases give about 85% coverage.
limits: Greedy set-cover style result, so the guarantee is a bound, not optimality. Needs the whole candidate pool in advance. A streaming agent sees cases one at a time.
agent_relevance: Cases have strongly diminishing returns. After the first few, each new case adds little. This justifies a novelty gate at write time.

source: Yang & Zhu (2001) A case-addition policy for case-base maintenance, Computational Intelligence 17(2)
finding: Experiment on Towers of Hanoi (four disks, 81 states, 6561 possible problems). 200 random planning cases cover 5649 of the 6561 problems (86%). The greedy addition algorithm reaches full coverage with only 58 cases. The first 10 cases already cover 73%, and the last 38 cases add only about 10%. Addition also beat the Smyth and Keane deletion policy at equal sizes.
numbers: Coverage by size: 1 case 12%, 5 cases 50%, 10 cases 73%, 20 cases 90%, 30 cases 96%, 58 cases 100%. First case benefit 676 problems. Adaptation-cost limit L = 2.
limits: One synthetic planning domain where coverage is exactly computable. A second path-finding domain was also run (not read in detail).
agent_relevance: Direct measured evidence that a small, well chosen case set matches a large random one: 58 chosen versus 200 random cases.

source: Pan, Yang, Pan, Li (2005) Competence driven case-base mining (AAAI-05)
finding: Shows that the Smyth and Keane deletion policy is sensitive to noisy cases and keeps rare outlier cases as pivotal, which wastes space. Their kernel-based greedy case-mining algorithm (KGCM) uses Fisher discriminant analysis to pick statistically meaningful pivotal cases and a nonlinear kernel to enlarge coverage. It outperforms earlier coverage-based methods on a spiral data set and on UCI sets.
numbers: Competence measured as 1-NN accuracy against case-base size ratio. KGCM rises fastest toward the optimum when size goes from 1% to 5%; a noise-ratio sweep on the spiral set shows the deletion approach degrading. Exact numbers are in figures that did not extract as text.
quote: deletion-based algorithm is sensitive to noisy cases
limits: Classification data sets only, not open problem solving. Numeric figures were not readable from the extracted text, so only the qualitative direction is recorded.
agent_relevance: A pivotal case may just be noise. In an LLM setting, a lone successful trace could be a lucky guess. Do not treat uniqueness alone as value; require the outcome to be checked.

source: Guo, Du, Chen, Chang, Wang (2026) CASCADE: Case-Based Continual Adaptation for Large Language Models During Deployment
finding: CASCADE defines deployment-time learning: a frozen LLM improves from a stream of tasks with only a binary success or failure signal. It follows the CBR 4R cycle. Retrieval is a contextual bandit (Neural-LinLogUCB). The retention rule is simple: store the new case (query, answer, reward) only if the reward is 1; otherwise the case bank is unchanged.
numbers: 16 tasks across medical diagnosis, legal analysis, code, web search, tool use, embodied interaction. Abstract claims +20.9% macro-averaged success rate over zero-shot. Retention rule: M(t+1) = M(t) union {(q,a,r)} if r=1, else M(t).
quote: successful new cases are retained in the case bank
limits: The retention rule is fixed; it is not compared against other retention rules in the paper. The reward must be trusted binary feedback.
agent_relevance: This is the success-only baseline policy our S9 step is measured against. It needs a trustworthy pass/fail check, which matches our guardrail G3.

source: Guo, Du, Chen, Chang, Wang (2026) CASCADE: Case-Based Continual Adaptation for Large Language Models During Deployment
finding: Regret is split into coverage gap (no good case is stored) and retrieval regret (a good case exists but the retriever misses it). The Retain step controls only the coverage gap. A theorem bounds the accumulated coverage gap as sub-linear: O~(T^((d0-1)/d0)) when intrinsic dimension d0 > 1, and O~(1) when d0 <= 1.
numbers: Assumptions: similar queries have similar solutions (Lipschitz), the LLM succeeds with probability at least p_min > 0 even with an irrelevant case, and queries are i.i.d. with a density condition. Theorem 4 gives t0 = (8/p_min) log(32/p_min)+1 and a bound with the sum of (t-1)^(-1/d0).
limits: The assumptions are strong: i.i.d. queries and a nonzero chance of success for every query. The authors call the p_min assumption a technical simplification. Real task streams drift.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean reason to keep only verified successes: every kept case shrinks the uncovered query space. It also says the benefit falls as the bank fills, matching the addition-policy result.

source: Guo, Du, Chen, Chang, Wang (2026) CASCADE: Case-Based Continual Adaptation for Large Language Models During Deployment
finding: Ablation on 12 single-turn tasks with Qwen3-32B (5 seeds each). Zero-shot averages 48.33. The non-adaptive case-based baseline NP-CBR (retain successes, retrieve by similarity) averages 63.76. Full CASCADE averages 66.68. So most of the gain (15.4 of 18.4 points) comes from simply retaining successful cases, and 2.9 points from learned retrieval.
numbers: Average success: Zero-shot 48.33; NP-CBR 63.76; w/o exploration 66.37; LinLogUCB 63.95; NeuralLogUCB 65.39; NeuralLinUCB 65.49; full 66.68. Largest single gains over zero-shot: MIMIC-IV-MR 12.79 to 63.98; RCA 45.36 to 70.76; MUD 25.53 to 62.44.
limits: The ablation varies retrieval, not retention. It shows how much success-only retention alone is worth but not whether a better retention rule would add more.
agent_relevance: Retention of verified successes is the main source of the gain. The retrieval learning on top is a smaller add-on.

source: Guo, Du, Chen, Chang, Wang (2026) CASCADE: Case-Based Continual Adaptation for Large Language Models During Deployment
finding: Across model sizes, CASCADE beats zero-shot on average in every size tested. Averages (12 single-turn tasks): Qwen3-8B 43.22 zero-shot, 58.44 NP-CBR, 60.84 CASCADE; Qwen3-14B 48.33, 62.81, 65.10; Qwen3-32B 48.33, 63.76, 66.68. The black-box gemini-2.0-flash also gains on all nine usable tasks.
numbers: Table S4. Qwen3-8B: ICRL 43.59 and ICRLPlus 46.76 are far below NP-CBR 58.44; REINFORCE+LoRA 54.47. Qwen3-32B: REINFORCE+LoRA 58.93 vs CASCADE 66.68. Gemini: CASCADE about +3% relative over NP-CBR. 5 seeds, std shown in table.
limits: Table text is partly garbled in extraction; the Qwen3-4B row is incomplete. Task set is the authors' own benchmark (DTLBench).
agent_relevance: A memory of verified cases beat weight updates (LoRA RL) in the same stream setting. This supports memory over fine-tuning for a scaffold-only agent.

source: Guo, Du, Chen, Chang, Wang (2026) CASCADE: Case-Based Continual Adaptation for Large Language Models During Deployment
finding: Limits stated by the authors. (1) Long-horizon behaviour is untested: memory growth, case management and forgetting are future work. (2) CASCADE learns only from successes and discards failures that may carry signal. (3) It needs some base ability: when zero-shot success is near zero, learning from experience is much harder.
numbers: MIMIC-IV-MR Qwen3-8B zero-shot is 5.94 and still reaches 54.88 with CASCADE, so low is not zero; Qwen3-4B could not run on MIMIC-IV-MR at all.
quote: the current framework primarily learns from successful experiences, discarding failed attempts that may contain informative signals
limits: These are the authors' own stated limits, not a measured test. No experiment varies the retention policy.
agent_relevance: The paper leaves open exactly our subfield: which cases to store beyond successes only, and when to forget. Open question for S9.

source: Guo, Du, Chen, Chang, Wang (2026) CASCADE: Case-Based Continual Adaptation for Large Language Models During Deployment
finding: Human-in-the-loop test: if a human can always supply a correct case (retain probability 1), the coverage gap closes faster and most tasks improve. But some tasks got worse (MIMIC-MR, MIMIC-MSR, CMDL, LFD), because the retriever could not handle a case bank that grew large and diverse within the limited steps.
numbers: Four of 12 tasks degraded under always-retain with ground-truth cases. Multi-case retrieval: REINFORCE+LoRA beat single-case CASCADE on 3 of 12 tasks (MIMIC-IV-MSR, MIMIC-IV-TLP, LFD); the gap closed at 4 retrieved cases.
limits: Short online horizon. The harm may fade with more steps or a better retriever; not tested.
agent_relevance: Even correct cases can hurt if the bank grows faster than retrieval can use it. Retaining more is not always better. Keep a size or novelty gate.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior
finding: First systematic LLM-agent test of memory addition and deletion. Agents show an experience-following property: the more similar a retrieved record's input is to the new task, the more similar the agent's output is to the stored output (Pearson r near 1 in RegAgent). This makes stored errors spread (error propagation) and makes stale records mislead (misaligned experience replay).
numbers: Four agents: RegAgent (synthetic), EHRAgent, AgentDriver (nuScenes), CIC-IoT Agent. Fixed-memory baselines start at 100, 100, 180 and 50 records. Several LLM backbones, including GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3, show the same pattern.
limits: The authors say they give empirical results only, with no theoretical guarantee. The strict evaluator uses ground truth.
agent_relevance: If retrieved cases are copied closely, one bad stored case is repeated in later outputs. Store only checked cases and mark provenance.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior
finding: Addition test (Table 1). Add-all (store every execution) is worse than the fixed starting memory on all four agents. A coarse automatic judge helps only if good enough. A strict judge using ground truth is best on all four.
numbers: RegAgent success / EHRAgent accuracy / AgentDriver success / CIC-IoT accuracy: Fixed 67.53 / 16.75 / 40.11 / 71.50; Add-all 55.48 / 13.05 / 32.32 / 59.90 (memory 4100 / 2411 / 2125 / 1050 records); coarse judge C1 63.18 / 26.19 / 36.92 / 74.00; C2 65.78 / 32.21 / 40.01 / 68.80; C3 (judge fine-tuned on 300 trajectories) 67.35 / 34.66 / 47.37 / 79.50; Strict 70.95 / 38.50 / 51.00 / 85.40.
limits: Strict evaluator uses ground-truth error thresholds, so it is an oracle-like filter not available in open deployment. Single reported run per cell.
agent_relevance: Indiscriminate writing lowers accuracy by 8 to 12 points versus a frozen start. A good filter lifts it 3 to 22 points above. Retention quality beats retention volume.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior
finding: Deletion test (Table 2). Three rules: periodical (time-based decay), history-based (remove records whose later retrievals led to poor outputs, a utility score), and combined. With a strict judge, history-based deletion keeps nearly all accuracy while shrinking memory a little. Periodical and combined deletion cut memory by about 3x with a small loss. With a noisy judge, history-based deletion can hurt.
numbers: Coarse judge C1, RegAgent: no deletion 63.18 (3511 records), periodic 60.88 (1012), history 62.10 (3205), combined 59.32 (951). Strict judge, RegAgent: no deletion 70.95 (2938), periodic 67.65 (949), history 69.80 (2286), combined 66.58 (890). CIC-IoT strict: 85.40 (904) no deletion, 80.80 (310) periodic.
limits: Mixed picture: the authors say history-based deletion gave the best result for real agents with a strict judge, but in the synthetic RegAgent it only trailed no deletion slightly. Some cells were hard to read from the PDF text.
agent_relevance: Pruning to about a third of the records costs only 3 to 5 points. Deletion by observed downstream harm works only when the harm signal is reliable.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior
finding: Extra conditions. (1) Under task distribution shift, strict addition still works and periodic deletion helps stabilise (on EHRAgent history-based deletion lagged combined deletion). (2) With a hard memory cap equal to the starting size (100 for EHRAgent, 180 for AgentDriver), managed memory still beats the fixed memory. (3) In AgentDriver, history-based deletion with a strict judge beat the error-free-memory baseline.
numbers: Capped memory sizes 100 (EHRAgent) and 180 (AgentDriver). Performance converges as the cap rises, so unbounded growth is unnecessary.
limits: The error-free memory baseline replaces the model's output with the ground truth in stored records; built only for AgentDriver and RegAgent.
agent_relevance: Supports a small bounded case store with periodic pruning plus a quality filter.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Memento is a case-based planner for deep research agents. It retains BOTH successful and failed trajectories as (state, plan, reward) triplets. The write step appends every case. A learned Q-function over cases then filters at read time, so the system does not decide at write time what to leave out.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88% (top-1 on validation) with memory built over three passes; test 79.40% (4th) using only the validation-built case bank. HLE 24.4% PM; SimpleQA 95.0%.
limits: Different task set and models than CASCADE (GPT-4.1 planner, o3 or o4-mini executor), so numbers are not comparable. Case counts per condition not clearly reported in the text read.
agent_relevance: Opposite design to CASCADE: store everything with its outcome label, and let retrieval learn which cases help. A design option for S9.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Learning curve over five passes on DeepResearcher: non-parametric CBR and parametric (Q-learned) CBR beat the same planner without case memory at each pass. The authors looked for an inflexion where more cases hurt and found none, because the bank saturates quickly (about 3k training tasks).
numbers: Iterations 1 to 5, Memento w/o CBR: 78.65, 80.93, 82.62, 83.53, 84.47. Non-parametric CBR: 79.84, 81.87, 83.09, 84.03, 84.85. Parametric CBR: 80.46, 82.84, 84.10, 84.85, 85.44. Gain over no-CBR at iteration 5: +0.38 (non-param), +0.97 (param).
limits: The no-CBR curve also rises, so the case-memory part is under 1 point by pass 5. Finite benchmark, so the authors could not test long-run decline.
agent_relevance: Retention gains here are small and shrink with passes: diminishing returns, the same shape as the Hanoi coverage curve.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Ablation across benchmarks: adding case memory helps or hurts depending on task. The authors report that on open-domain data one component hurt (DeepResearcher: -18.0 F1 / -2.1 PM), while on SimpleQA and HLE the same component helped. Planning gives the more robust gains.
numbers: Reported deltas: SimpleQA +28.8 F1 / +63.3 PM; HLE +4.8 / +7.1; DeepResearcher -18.0 / -2.1. These belong to one ablation step (the text read says the effect may even hurt on open-domain data); which exact step is not certain from the extracted text.
limits: I could not map every delta to a named condition from the extracted text. Treat the attribution with care.
agent_relevance: Memory benefit is task dependent. Measure per task before assuming stored cases help.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: AWM stores abstracted workflows (reusable sub-routines) induced from experience, not raw trajectories. Online, it induces workflows from the agent's own past test trajectories judged successful by an evaluator. Reported gains: +24.6% relative on WebArena and +51.1% on Mind2Web. The agent learns fast in the first 40 or so examples, then plateaus.
numbers: WebArena +24.6% relative task success; Mind2Web +51.1% relative. Online learning curve: rapid between 0 and 40 examples. One analysis: workflows used by 0.94 of test examples; only 0.08 overlap between steps of different workflows. About 2.0 fewer steps per example than the BrowserGym baseline.
limits: Online mode induces from model-predicted trajectories that may be wrong; the authors note incorrect workflows can degrade performance. Offline and online perform comparably in-domain; online generalises better when train and test domains differ.
agent_relevance: Abstracting before storing (workflow, not trace) is a third retention form. Its weakness matches CASCADE's: it depends on a correct success judgement.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory, rule-based induction variant (appendix)
finding: A non-LLM retention filter in the appendix: deduplicate experiences, then drop invalid actions (actions that cannot execute because arguments do not fit). This is a cheap code-checked write gate.
numbers: Two steps: experience deduplication, invalid-action filtering. No separate headline number was recorded from this section.
limits: Appendix variant; the main results use LLM-based induction.
agent_relevance: Matches our rule that code, not the model, decides. A dedup plus validity check can run before any case is stored.

source: Zhao et al. (2023) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: ExpeL gathers experience with retries, keeps success and failure pairs, and extracts natural-language insights by comparing a failure with a success. Only successful trajectories go into the recall store; insights come from both. Experience matters: extracting insights from the starting few-shot examples alone gave no gain over plain ReAct.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieval-only: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%, ALFWorld 50% vs 55%. Matches Reflexion on HotpotQA (40% at R3 vs 39%) and beats it on ALFWorld without repeat attempts. Agents that gathered diverse success-failure pairs (via Reflexion) beat those using plain ReAct for gathering.
limits: Single benchmark for the experience-quantity test (HotpotQA). Insight and recall effects differ by environment.
agent_relevance: Keep failures for contrast, but store them as comparisons with a success, not as stand-alone cases to copy.

source: Chhikara et al. (2025) Mem0: building production-ready AI agents with scalable long-term memory
finding: Mem0 uses an LLM to decide, for each extracted fact, one of the operations against the existing store: ADD (no equivalent memory), UPDATE (add complementary info), DELETE (contradicted), or no-op. This is a write-time dedup and conflict gate. On LOCOMO it cuts p95 latency by over 91% against full-context.
numbers: LOCOMO benchmark: 10 conversations, about 600 dialogues and 26000 tokens each. Relative gains of 5%, 11% and 7% on single-hop, temporal and multi-hop questions over the best other method; Mem0 about 67% J score, Mem0g over 68%.
limits: Conversation memory, not problem-solving cases. The write decision is by an LLM, which our schema forbids as the sole judge (G5).
agent_relevance: Shows the dedup/update/delete vocabulary for the write gate. We would implement the equivalence test in code, with an LLM only filling a slot.

source: Aha, Kibler, Albert (1991) Instance-based learning algorithms (Machine Learning 6), pointer only
finding: Early instance-based retention rule (IB2/IB3): store a new instance only if the current memory misclassifies it, and drop instances that prove poor predictors. Not opened here; recorded from memory as a pointer for the next pass.
numbers: No numbers recorded because the paper was not opened.
limits: Unverified this session. Open it in a later pass before relying on it.
agent_relevance: A store-only-the-surprises rule maps to: store a case only when no stored case solved it. Test as a candidate S9 gate.

source: Synthesis of retention-rule families across the sources above
finding: Five retention rules appear in the sources: (1) store everything (add-all; Memento write); (2) store only verified successes (CASCADE); (3) store only the novel or uncovered (coverage-based addition, IB-style); (4) delete by use-utility (Minton, history-based deletion); (5) delete by coverage uniqueness (footprint). Only Xiong et al. and Smyth and Keane compare rules head to head.
numbers: Head-to-head numbers: Smyth and Keane, competence 100% (footprint) vs 80% (utility) vs 86% (random). Xiong et al., add-all lowers accuracy by 8 to 12 points vs fixed memory (RegAgent 55.48 vs 67.53; CIC-IoT 59.90 vs 71.50).
limits: Our own synthesis; no study compares success-only, novelty-only and store-all in one LLM stream. That is a gap.
agent_relevance: Candidate S9 policy to test: store a verified success only if the nearest stored neighbour did not already solve it; store a failure only paired with the later fix; prune by coverage, then by observed harm.
